case_study_insert.main_stem: Kirkstone Quarry Products (KQP) is a private limited company in the construction aggregates sector, employing a workforce of 60. Founded in 1998 by Duncan Kirkstone, it supplies crushed rock to regional road builders and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership on its quarry site. KQP plans to invest $960,000 in a mobile crushing and screening plant that produces recycled aggregate from demolition waste, financed by a $600,000 ten-year bank loan and $360,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $420,000 a year, a variable cost of $9.00 a unit and a selling price of $16.00, and currently produces 84,000 units a year. KQP faces two problems: the reject rate on crushed stone is 2.4% after rework, and dust complaints from nearby residents are rising.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quarterly Operations Log, Q4 2025: the mobile crusher processed 21,000 tonnes at a reject rate of 2.4%, down from 4.0% a year earlier. Dust-suppression complaints from nearby residents fell from 17 to 9 per month. Average lorry turnaround is 38 minutes. Market research of 400 local builders found that 58% would pay up to $0.50 more per tonne for recycled aggregate, and 46% check for eco-certification when ordering. A skills audit shows 14 of 60 site staff are not certified on the new screening plant; external accreditation courses cost $750 per operative.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Kirkstone Quarry Products for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank lifted the base rate from 4.25% to 5.0%, raising borrowing costs on variable-rate business loans. (2) The national minimum wage rises 5.8% from $13.00 to $13.75 an hour from April 2026, lifting site wage bills. (3) Diesel and tyre input costs for haulage have risen 9.5% year-on-year while construction-sector inflation is 6.2% and public infrastructure spending grew 2.8%.

questions.question_text: KQP plans to fund part of its $960,000 crushing-plant expansion with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for KQP of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Using retained profit costs KQP nothing in interest or capital repayments, which protects cash flow at a time when the quarry already carries fixed costs of $420,000 a year and a $600,000 bank loan. Every dollar not paid to the lender can be kept to absorb the 9.5% rise in diesel and tyre costs, helping KQP hold its $16.00 selling price while it brings the new screening plant into use and tries to cut the 2.4% reject rate.

Point 2: Retained profit avoids the collateral and repossession risk that come with a bank loan, so the $360,000 is available without putting KQP's $960,000 crushing plant at risk if road-building demand falls. It also leaves Duncan Kirkstone's ownership untouched, since no outside lender can impose covenants on how the recycled aggregate operation is run or how quickly the remaining expansion is financed.

For KQP this matters because the plant must first turn demolition feedstock into saleable recycled aggregate before any of the $0.50 premium is earned; retained profit gives it time to reach 84,000 units without adding interest to the $420,000 fixed costs.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to KQP's retained profit, loan and fixed costs.

questions.question_text: KQP is launching its recycled aggregate range. Consider a national television campaign, regional radio advertising, or trade exhibitions with technical brochures. Which should KQP choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National television: A national TV campaign would build awareness of recycled aggregate with millions of viewers very quickly, but almost all of that audience are not buyers of quarried stone. For a 60-employee business already funding a $960,000 plant, the airtime and production spend would be largely wasted, and TV cannot demonstrate the technical specification that builders demand before specifying aggregate.

Regional radio: Radio is much cheaper and can reach the regional road builders and local contractors KQP already supplies, and it suits short time-limited messages. However, it is still a broad, audio-only medium: it cannot show the 46% of surveyed builders who check eco-certification the evidence they want, and its reach is too local to support the 84,000-unit output the new crusher is meant to fill.

Trade exhibitions and technical brochures: These reach the 400 builders in KQP's own research directly, of whom 58% would pay $0.50 more for recycled aggregate and 46% check eco-certification. Staff can show test data, explain how the reject rate has fallen to 2.4%, and take orders on the spot at modest cost relative to the $960,000 investment. Results build more slowly than TV and depend on KQP winning stand space, but the audience is precisely the buyer group.

Recommendation: KQP should choose trade exhibitions with technical brochures. They target the researched 400 builders, prove the eco credentials that 46% demand, and cost far less than television, which is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted. Radio is rejected because it cannot demonstrate certification or reach beyond the local catchment. KQP should add follow-up direct mail to existing contractors to convert the 58% premium signal.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the three promotional options with little reference to KQP.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options with some application to KQP's builders and budget.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three options with a justified recommendation that explains why television and radio are rejected.

questions.question_text: KQP operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership on its quarry site. Explain two benefits for KQP of this approach in managing safety and output.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A hierarchical structure gives KQP a clear chain of command and a narrow span of control on a dangerous quarry site, so safety rules for the crushing and screening plant are set once and passed down without ambiguity. With heavy mobile equipment and 60 site staff, a single accountable manager can enforce dust controls and machine guarding, which helps KQP address the rising dust complaints and keeps the 2.4% reject rate from turning into a serious incident.

Point 2: Autocratic leadership allows fast, decisive instructions when the crusher jams or a lorry schedule slips, without waiting for consultation across the workforce of 60. That speed protects the throughput needed to reach 84,000 units a year and helps KQP service the $600,000 bank loan on time. Clear top-down direction also makes it easier to impose the new operating routines for the $960,000 screening plant, so the recycled aggregate line reaches full capacity quickly rather than drifting through an informal rollout.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to KQP's quarry safety, output and structure.

questions.question_text: KQP must close its skills gap: 14 of 60 site staff are not certified on the new screening plant. Consider on-the-job training or external accreditation courses at $750 per operative. Which should KQP choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching at the crusher is specific to KQP's own screening plant and quality standards, costs no course fees, and keeps all 14 operatives productive while they learn, protecting the 84,000-unit output target and the improvement that brought the reject rate down to 2.4%. Its weaknesses are that trainers are themselves site staff whose work is interrupted, bad habits can be copied, and there is no formal certificate, which matters because 46% of surveyed builders check eco-certification and may ask to see operator records.

External accreditation: Paying $750 for each of the 14 uncertified staff costs 14 × $750 = $10,500, a small fraction of the $960,000 investment. Accreditation gives a recognised credential, reinforces the eco-certification message that builders value, and brings an outside standard that could push the 2.4% reject rate lower. However, it removes 14 of 60 workers from the site temporarily, reducing crusher availability, and the generic course may not match KQP's exact plant settings, so some on-site follow-up would still be required.

Decision: KQP should choose external accreditation for all 14 operatives. Safety on a quarry and the eco-certification demanded by 46% of builders make a formal, recognised credential worth the $10,500 and the short loss of site capacity. On-the-job training is rejected as the main answer because it cannot provide the certificate those customers check and risks passing on the very habits that caused the 2.4% rejects; KQP should add brief on-site coaching afterwards to cover machine-specific settings.

The $10,500 is also tiny beside the $960,000 capital cost, so formal certification is a low-risk way to protect the 84,000-unit output and the falling 2.4% reject rate.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with little KQP context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analysis of benefits and drawbacks of one or both methods applied to KQP's 14 staff and costs.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods with a justified decision that rejects the alternative and uses the $10,500 computation.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how KQP's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $420,000 ÷ ($16.00 − $9.00) = $420,000 ÷ $7.00 = 60,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 60,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $16.00 − $9.00 = $7.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $7.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways KQP's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 60,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 84,000 units to confirm a margin of safety of 24,000 units, showing how far sales could fall before the $960,000 plant stops paying.
2. Use the $7.00 contribution per unit to model a discount for road builders: a $0.50 a tonne concession still leaves $6.50 contribution, so managers can judge whether extra volume would cover the $420,000 fixed costs.
3. Set the volume needed to service the $600,000 bank loan: at 84,000 units the business is well above break-even, so managers can test whether a downturn would still leave enough cash for loan payments.
4. Benchmark unit cost of $14.00 ($420,000 ÷ 84,000 units + $9.00) each quarter; a rising figure would signal the 2.4% rejects or waste are eroding profitability and prompt action.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 60,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $7.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses: 24,000-unit margin of safety vs 84,000 output; $0.50 discount modelling against $420,000 fixed costs; servicing the $600,000 loan; and $14.00 unit-cost benchmarking to track the 2.4% rejects.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for the accurate answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied use in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate KQP's profitability. Has KQP's profitability improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 40.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 45.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 12.5%
Profit Margin 2025 = 16.5%
ROCE 2024 = 15.0%
ROCE 2025 = 21.0%

Detailed workings: Revenue rose from $1,200,000 to $1,400,000 while cost of sales increased only from $720,000 to $770,000, so gross profit grew from $480,000 to $630,000. Operating profit climbed from $150,000 to $231,000 and capital employed from $1,000,000 to $1,100,000; interest payable was $18,000 then $22,000.

Evaluation: All three measures moved favourably. The 40.0% to 45.0% improvement in gross margin shows KQP is keeping quarrying and haulage costs contained as the new crusher cuts the reject rate to 2.4%. Operating margin rose from 12.5% to 16.5% because operating profit grew far faster than revenue, reflecting fixed-cost leverage as output approaches 84,000 units. Returns on capital improved from 15.0% to 21.0%, so the $960,000 screening plant is already earning more per dollar employed, even after $22,000 of interest. The caveat is that revenue growth of about 17% depends on road-building demand; if public infrastructure spending slows, the higher fixed base could reverse these gains quickly.

Conclusion: KQP's profitability has clearly improved: gross margin, operating margin and ROCE all rose together, so the investment is paying off. The main residual risk is dependence on construction demand, so KQP should lock in long-term aggregate contracts to protect the 45.0% gross margin.

Cost of sales rose only modestly relative to revenue, so the gain is not purely a volume effect: better control on the line running at a 2.4% reject rate is lowering unit costs, which makes the improvement durable rather than a single favourable quarter.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States figures or changes with little or no accurate calculation.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates margins and returns for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years plus detailed evaluation of revenue, costs and capital and a justified conclusion on whether profitability improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for KQP of using recycled construction aggregate from demolition waste in its operations.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Recycled aggregate matches a clear market signal: 58% of the 400 surveyed builders would pay $0.50 more and 46% check eco-certification, so KQP can protect its $7.00 contribution per unit and win road contracts even as diesel and tyre costs rise 9.5%. It also builds a greener brand that may satisfy public infrastructure buyers.

Disadvantage: Recycled material is more variable in quality than fresh crushed rock, so processing it may lift the current 2.4% reject rate and add rework cost. Sorting and screening demolition waste also pushes up the $9.00 variable cost per unit, which would squeeze margins unless the $0.50 premium is accepted across the whole 84,000-unit output. Early supply of clean demolition feedstock is not guaranteed.

To make the advantage real, KQP must secure a steady supply of clean demolition waste so sorting does not push the 2.4% reject rate up; doing so also spreads the $420,000 fixed costs over more of the 84,000 units.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development using KQP's research, costs and reject data.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base rate rise to 5.0%, the 5.8% minimum wage increase and the 9.5% rise in diesel and tyre costs will affect KQP. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.0%): If KQP's $600,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, the annual interest bill rises by 0.75% of $600,000 = $4,500 a year (0.0075 × $600,000). That is small beside fixed costs of $420,000 and could be removed by fixing the rate. Higher base rates may also make road-building clients cautious and raise the cost of any future borrowing, but the direct cash effect is modest and controllable.

Minimum wage increase (5.8%, to $13.75 an hour): With a workforce of 60, much of the site and haulage work is hourly paid, so this rise feeds into costs and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay, so no honest annual wage total can be invented. The defensible comparison is productivity: 84,000 units ÷ 60 staff = 1,400 units per worker, so a wage rise is affordable only while that productivity holds or output grows; otherwise unit labour cost climbs and the $7.00 contribution per unit narrows.

Diesel and tyre costs (9.5%): These hit every lorry movement and every tonne crushed. The insert does not split the $9.00 variable cost, so only a labelled bound is honest: if the whole variable cost rose 9.5%, that adds 9.5% × $9.00 = $0.86 a unit (about $0.855), or roughly 84,000 × $0.855 = $71,820 a year. Even a smaller pass-through would materially reduce the $7.00 contribution that must cover $420,000 fixed costs and service the $960,000 investment.

Conclusion: The 9.5% rise in diesel and tyre costs will have the greatest impact. It compounds across all 84,000 units, directly erodes the contribution that justifies the crushing plant, and cannot be fixed by a simple rate swap. The interest rise is small and fixable, and the wage rise can be absorbed if the 1,400-units-per-worker productivity holds, so both are secondary.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited KQP application.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on KQP's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes with a well-justified judgement that diesel and tyre inflation has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.
